analysis.one_liner: Extends online privacy protections to teenagers and restricts targeted ads aimed at kids and teens.
analysis.headline: The bill to strengthen children's online privacy never left a House subcommittee; it ended the Congress with no cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would update a 1998 law that protects kids' data online. It would extend those protections to 13-to-15-year-olds, require websites and apps aimed at young people to get consent before collecting their personal information, ban targeted advertising to children outright and to teens without the teen's consent, give parents and teens the right to see and delete collected data, and bar the sale of internet-connected toys and devices aimed at kids unless they meet federal cybersecurity standards. It was introduced in July 2019, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers using websites, apps, and internet-connected devices, plus their parents, who would get notice and control over what personal data is collected, a right to have inaccurate data corrected or erased, and protection from targeted advertising based on a young person's profile. Families buying connected toys and devices would get a standardized privacy label on the packaging.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the online privacy protections that today apply only to children under 13 to minors aged 13 to 15, covering websites, online services, online applications, and mobile applications directed at them or that know a user is a minor.

Requires operators to get verifiable consent before collecting a child's or minor's personal information, and bans conditioning use of a service on handing over more personal information than is needed to participate.
Prohibits targeted marketing to children outright, and to minors unless the minor consents; the bill also bars profiling children by race or socioeconomic status to direct content at them.

Gives parents and minors the right to request a description of the personal information collected, delete it, and challenge and correct inaccurate information, and requires operators to keep reasonable security procedures for that data.

Requires a standardized privacy dashboard on the packaging of internet-connected devices aimed at children and minors, and bans selling such devices unless they meet FTC-set cybersecurity and data security standards.
Lets state attorneys general sue to enforce the law and obtain restitution for residents, and expands FTC enforcement to telecommunications carriers and cable operators.

analysis.who_pays: Online platforms, advertising technology companies, and consumer data brokers would bear compliance costs and lose revenue from tracking and targeted advertising to young users. Manufacturers of internet-connected devices aimed at children would face new security testing, standards compliance, and labeling requirements.

drawbacks.text: Coverage hinges on whether a site is 'directed to' children or minors and on the operator's knowledge of a user's age, so general-audience platforms where most teens actually spend time could avoid the duties unless they take steps to verify age — a gap the bill partly addresses by deeming mixed-audience services covered only if they collect data before checking age.

The bill includes safe-harbor provisions letting companies comply through industry-drafted self-regulatory guidelines approved by the FTC, a route that could water down protections; the bill responds with Inspector General audits and mandatory publication of compliance reports.

Companies would face meaningful compliance costs, including FTC rulemakings within a year of enactment, per-device penalties for noncompliant connected devices, and penalties allowed above normal statutory caps on first violations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections for young people's data are substantial and aimed at a real, documented problem — commercial tracking and targeted advertising of minors. The main honest objections are enforcement coverage (teens on general-audience platforms may slip through) and the self-regulatory safe harbor that could blunt the rules, though the bill pairs the safe harbor with audits. On balance the benefits to families outweigh the compliance costs, which fall on companies profiting from the data collection being restricted.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Consumer Protection and Commerce subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Rush (D-IL) introduced the bill on July 23, 2019.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and the next day to the subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce.
No further action was taken; the bill received zero cosponsors and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online platforms, advertising technology firms, and makers of internet-connected children's devices are better off: they face no new restrictions on collecting and monetizing young users' data. Children and teens gained nothing, because the protections never became law.

for.name: Rep. Bobby L. Rush
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strengthen the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act on July 23, 2019.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never attracted enough support to reveal a partisan split: it had a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and no votes on record.

industries.industry: Online platforms and social media companies
industries.note: The bill would restrict collecting, using, and selling the personal data of users under 16 on services directed at or knowingly used by young people, and would ban targeted advertising to children and require teen consent for targeted ads. Platforms' advertising revenue depends on exactly this tracking.

The bill bars compiling or disclosing young users' personal information for targeted marketing and defines targeted marketing broadly to include profiling by demographics, psychology, or device identifiers. Their core business of profiling users for ad delivery would be curtailed for this population.

Device makers would have to meet FTC cybersecurity and data security standards before selling products aimed at children and minors and display a standardized privacy dashboard on packaging. That raises costs but also gives compliant makers a leg up over rivals selling insecure devices, and it directly protects families from insecure connected toys.
